name: ffni_mediation
title: FFNI Mediation: Follower Needs between Context and Leader Endorsement
description: Do fundamental follower needs mediate the effect of situational threat on the endorsement of dominance- versus prestige-based leaders? Sheng, Andrews & van Vugt (2026, docs/2027-27008-001.pdf, journal page numbers) validated the FFNI and named the gaps this design addresses: (1) mediation, p.795: prior work 'often assume yet do not empirically test the mediating role of follower needs'; (2) moderation, p.789: 'would intergroup conflict situations (e.g., trade wars, organizational crises) strengthen the FFN protection-authoritarianism link?'; (3) manipulation, p.796: their design was 'entirely self-report measures and correlational designs', and they call for 'experimental manipulations (e.g., vignettes or simulations of threat, inequality, or uncertainty)'; (4) behavioural outcomes, p.795: they call for 'behavioral consequences of follower needs, such as voting in elections'. Two more are our inference, not the paper's: the prototype and effectiveness results come from different samples and countries, and no participant ever rated a leader they had watched. All six, quoted in full, are under Research gaps in docs/README.md. H1 and H2 are carried over from the prestige_dominance study; H3-H7 are new.
vote_prompt: Based on what you observed, who should lead this team?

collaborative.hypothesis: H1: Prestige receives more peer votes than Dominance

hypotheses.H2: Threat: Dominance > Prestige endorsement. EXPLORATORY, and a deliberate departure. The dominance-under-threat literature the paper cites (Laustsen & Petersen, 2017, 2020; Spisak et al., 2012) is about INTERGROUP conflict -- war, a rival group, contested status. The threat pool drawn from HiddenBench is environmental instead: floods, storms, evacuations, casualties. That still qualifies as a protection trigger under the paper's own definition (p.771 lists 'wars, pandemics, or other types of immediate threats'), but there is no outgroup and no status dimension, and some evidence points the other way -- impersonal disaster favouring competence, which is the prestige side. So a null here does NOT replicate a null in the paper, and this is stated in advance rather than after seeing the number.
hypotheses.H3: Threat raises the PROTECTION need relative to routine (within-persona baseline -> post). Protection only, not status: p.795 maps intergroup conflict to protection, economic inequality to fairness and status, and male-biased sex ratios to protection and status. The threat pool is immediate physical danger with no rival group and nothing to gain -- the cleanest possible protection trigger, and one that touches no status dimension at all. This prediction is SHARPER under the drawn tasks than it was under the hand-written consolidation scenario, which was intergroup and so arguably moved status too.
hypotheses.H4: Cognition layer: each need predicts the prototype dimensions Table 13 (Study 5, Sample B) gives it a significant incremental R2 on -- protection to Strength, status to Tyranny/Masculinity/Well-groomed, vision to Sensitivity/Dedication/Charisma/Creativity, expertise to Sensitivity/Charisma/Intelligence, fairness to Dedication/Intelligence/Ethics. AFFILIATION IS DELIBERATELY ABSENT: Table 13 gives it delta R2 of .00 or .01 on all eleven dimensions and significance on none, despite bivariate correlations up to .54, so an entry for it would be a guess dressed as a replication (design-log section 23). It stays in the regression as a control. This is the study's POSITIVE CONTROL -- the paper's own supported result.
hypotheses.H5: Evaluation layer, read on Model 2 of Table 3 (Study 5, Sample E: each need with the other five controlled) -- the same incremental statistic H4 reads from Table 13. Model 1 (the need alone) is not used: its betas include variance the needs share. SUPPORTED in Model 2: affiliation to Team-building .36*** and Benevolence .10*; vision to Vision communication .18**; expertise to Intellectual stimulation .13*; fairness to Moral character .25***. NOT SUPPORTED in Model 2 though significant in Model 1: protection to Safety .05 (Model 1 .20***), vision to High-expectation .10 (.28***), expertise to Competence .08 (.22***), fairness to Virtue .08 (.26***). NOT SUPPORTED in either model: protection to Authoritarianism .01, status to Narcissism .04 / Authoritarianism -.02 / Dominance .02. So once the other needs are controlled, protection has no unique link to the effectiveness of any style -- Safety, its closest match, included -- while it keeps a unique link to the Strength prototype (beta .26, Table 13). A protection-to-D null here replicates that. Rating one observed person on one item cannot separate Safety from Authoritarianism, but under Model 2 the paper has no protection link for that collapse to hide.
hypotheses.H6: Protection need mediates the condition -> Dominance-endorsement effect (named as untested)
hypotheses.H7: Threat strengthens the protection -> dominance-side EVALUATION link. This is the paper's own open question, p.789: 'would intergroup conflict situations (e.g., trade wars, organizational crises) strengthen the FFN protection-authoritarianism link?' Authoritarianism is one of Table 3's effectiveness criteria, so the question is about the evaluation layer, and the quantity that answers it here is the between-condition difference in the protection -> Dominance-effectiveness beta. The second half this hypothesis used to carry -- that threat narrows the gap between the cognition and evaluation layers -- is this study's own extension and is not asked anywhere in the paper; it is kept as an exploratory quantity, not as a replication.

note: Scenarios are drawn per run from HiddenBench (Li, Naito & Shirado, arXiv:2505.11556, MIT), built by tools/fetch_hiddenbench.py. The threat manipulation is therefore which pool a run draws from, not prose we wrote -- and because every task has a correct answer, endorsement can be scored against whether the group actually decided well. Both conditions share one friction block for the same reason.
